messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Vignette:
Amara Osei is a 25-year-old Ghanaian-American surgical resident who presented for psychological evaluation approximately six weeks after returning from a medical humanitarian deployment in a conflict zone along the Horn of Africa. She arrived at the intake appointment composed and precise in her speech, though she sat with her chair pulled flush against the wall of the consulting room before she had even removed her coat, positioning herself so that the full length of the office was visible in front of her.

The event that brought her to treatment occurred during her fourth week of deployment, when the field hospital where she was stationed came under indirect fire. Amara had been mid-procedure — her gloved hands inside an abdominal cavity, managing hemorrhage in a soldier who had sustained shrapnel injuries — when the first explosion struck close enough to shake the surgical tent and send a fine grit of dust across the operative field. A second blast followed within seconds. The rotor noise of evacuation helicopters, which had been a constant background hum throughout the deployment, suddenly became deafening as two aircraft descended simultaneously in emergency extraction. In the chaos that followed, Amara continued operating for nearly forty minutes while the structure around her was partially evacuated, her hands moving through viscera and blood-soaked gauze, the specific wet, dense texture of packed surgical sponges pressing against her palms. She completed the procedure. The patient survived. She has not spoken about what those forty minutes were like to anyone.

That last detail is not incidental. Amara has found that the experience resists language entirely. When she has tried, in the weeks since returning, to explain what happened to her attending physician or to a friend who asked, the words simply do not come in any form that feels adequate or even accurate. She stops. She changes the subject. She has come to feel that attempting to describe it is not merely painful but somehow impossible, as though the event exists in a register that speech cannot reach.

What does reach her, without warning and without permission, are the triggers she cannot avoid. She works in a level-one trauma center in Atlanta, and the operating theater is a place where the texture of surgical sponges is an unremarkable daily constant. On two occasions since her return, the moment her gloved hands made contact with packed gauze, the full memory descended on her instantaneously — not as recollection but as reinstatement, carrying with it the identical terror she had experienced in the tent. She has said nothing to her supervising surgeons. She is certain that if they knew, her residency would be in jeopardy, and she has worked too long and sacrificed too much for that outcome. The same collapse of time and safety has occurred twice in the hospital parking structure when a medical helicopter passed low overhead on approach to the rooftop landing pad, and once in the hospital cafeteria when a door slammed at the far end of the room.

In the weeks following her return, Amara reorganized her daily life around a set of practices that felt, to her, less like avoidance than like elementary prudence. She now enters every room — the surgical lounge, the cafeteria, the elevator lobby — only after she has identified where the exits are and confirmed a clear path to them. She sits with her back against a solid surface whenever possible. She scans doorways and corridors continuously, her attention moving in a systematic sweep that she is aware her colleagues have begun to notice and find unusual. She has declined three social invitations since returning, each involving a restaurant or bar she had not visited before and therefore could not pre-assess. One of those invitations came from a fellow resident she had been close to during her intern year; he has not reached out again.

What finally compelled her to seek help was a moment in the scrub bay two weeks ago, when she looked down at her own hands under running water and could not, for a period she estimates at roughly thirty seconds, feel certain she was in Atlanta and not still in the tent. She made the appointment that afternoon. What she fears most is that something has been permanently altered in her capacity to function as a surgeon. What she hopes for, stated quietly at the close of the intake, is simply to be able to put her hands on a patient without bracing for the world to come apart.
